title: Working models for a trainer: employed, facility-contracted or independent
audience: Personal trainers and fitness professionals who are deciding how to work: as an employee, under a contract to a facility, or independently.
learningOutcomes: Compare employed, facility-contracted and independent working models using the same six criteria
Identify the costs and records each model places on the trainer, and list each Australian legal or tax point to be checked.
Choose a model for a stated situation and write the reasons and the trade-offs being accepted

instruction.heading: Three working models
instruction.body: A personal trainer can work in at least three broad ways. In the first, the trainer is employed by a gym, studio or other employer, who pays for time on the floor and a different rate for each training session. In the second, the trainer contracts their services to a facility and pays a fee per client or a monthly fee for the use of the space, carrying their own costs. In the third, the trainer runs an independent business, for example travelling to clients' homes or working from a studio they lease. Each model moves costs, risk and records between the trainer and someone else. The source describes the first two in detail. The third is an addition in this lesson and uses the same comparison method.

instruction.heading: What employment gives you, and what it takes
instruction.body: As an employee, marketing, equipment and facility costs usually sit with the employer. Some employers provide training, uniforms or group class opportunities, and some invite trainers to comment on equipment and layout. The trade-offs are real. Employers may set dress and grooming standards, minimum hours and sales goals, and the pay for each session can be lower than an independent trainer could earn. The source gives a pay share as a percentage of the client fee. That figure is not used, because it is not an Australian benchmark. The source's account of US employer tax reporting is NOT APPLICABLE in Australia and is not used.

instruction.heading: What a facility contract asks of you
instruction.body: Under a facility contract, the trainer pays a fee to use the space, per client or per month, and carries their own operating costs. The trainer also has no say over how the facility runs, so changes to the room, hours or policies are outside their control. The source suggests a newcomer may price a little under local competitors. That suggestion is not used here as a rule, because it has no Australian basis. Fees must cover the space, insurance, marketing, equipment, records and the trainer's own tax, so a rate that merely sounds cheap is not a plan. Training clients on a facility's premises without paying the facility is a serious breach. The source says this can lead to prosecution. The source also names a professional conduct code, which was not read for this lesson.

instruction.heading: What running your own business asks of you
instruction.body: An independent trainer sets fees from their experience and from what the local market will pay. They carry all marketing costs, all travel time between clients' homes, any health questionnaires and client release forms, and all record-keeping. They must also meet their tax obligations on earned income. Before you rely on any of them, check current official guidance, then speak with a registered accountant or an insurance broker (see “Professional advisers: when to ask, and what to bring”).

instruction.heading: Choose a model with the same criteria for each
instruction.body: Compare the three models on six criteria: the monthly income you need, how stable that income is, how much control you have over hours and location, the travel and admin load, the marketing cost you carry, and the records you must keep. Then check the working arrangement itself. Whether a worker is an employee or a contractor depends on how the work is actually done, not on what the agreement calls it.

procedure: Write the monthly income you need, and how many sessions it takes to earn it
Score each of the three models against the six criteria, with a note for each score
List the costs and records each model would place on you
Leave every Australian legal or tax point off the plan until it is checked.
Check the working arrangement for each model against the employee or contractor test
Choose one model, and record the reasons and the trade-offs you accept

workedExamples.situation: Mia has two years of training experience in a regional city. She is weighing a weekday role at a gym that pays per session, against building her own home-visit business with no fixed income in the first months.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which model should she compare first, and what must she record before deciding?
workedExamples.reasoning: She should score both models on the same six criteria, starting with the monthly income she needs and the sessions that give it. She should list the costs and records each model places on her, and list the Australian tax, insurance and registration points to be checked. She should check the working arrangement for each option using the employee or contractor test before she signs anything.

workedExamples.situation: Jared has little capital and wants to train clients this month. A facility offers him space at a fixed monthly fee, with no contract terms in writing yet.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should Jared confirm before his first client session?
workedExamples.reasoning: He should confirm the space arrangement in writing, including the fee, what it covers, the hours and the cancellation terms. He should price his sessions from his real costs, including the monthly fee, and he should not treat the source's pricing suggestion as a rule.

equipmentAndPpe: No PPE is needed for this lesson
A model comparison sheet with the six criteria
Any draft offers, space agreements or contracts for each model

commonErrors.error: Using the source's pay share or pricing suggestion as Australian benchmarks
commonErrors.prevention: Mark both as US and historical in your notes, and set your own rates from your costs and local evidence.

commonErrors.error: Assuming that a contractor label makes a worker a contractor
commonErrors.prevention: Check how the work is done against the test in “Deciding on your first team member”, and take advice where you are unsure.

commonErrors.error: Leaving travel, admin and marketing out when setting an independent rate
commonErrors.prevention: List every cost per session, including travel time, before you set a fee.

commonErrors.error: Training clients at a facility without paying for the space
commonErrors.prevention: Confirm the space arrangement in writing before the first client session.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not rely on them until they are checked against official guidance.
The source's account of how a worker's status is set is not used as an Australian rule.
NOT APPLICABLE: the source's US employer tax reporting, the W-2 form and US employment law. These are not Australian requirements and are not used.
Licence notice: this lesson does not grant any licence, certificate or registration for personal training work.

qualityStandard: The comparison uses the same six criteria for all three models
Every US figure in the source is marked US and historical, and is not used as an Australian benchmark
Each Australian legal or tax point is left out until it is checked.
The trade-offs of the chosen model are written into the record
documentationEvidence: Model comparison sheet with scores and notes
Monthly income target and the sessions it requires
Cost list per session for the chosen model
Record of the employee or contractor check and any advice taken
summary: Employment, facility contracts and independent work move costs and risk in different ways
Compare models on the same criteria, including income, control, travel, marketing and records
Figures from another country and an earlier period are not Australian benchmarks
Check the working arrangement, not only the label, and take advice on tax and insurance

knowledgeChecks.question: A trainer is offered per-session pay at a share of the client fee. What is the right first step?
options: Compare the offer with the costs of working independently, and check the Australian pay rules, which have not yet been confirmed in this lesson
Accept it, because the source describes that arrangement as normal and that is how most trainers are paid at every studio in the area
Refuse it without comparing, because all employed roles are poor value and the trainer has no other offers to consider at all

knowledgeChecks.question: Under a contract to use a facility, which costs does the trainer usually carry?
options: The facility's marketing and equipment and the front desk staff
The charge for access to the room, together with their own operating costs
The facility's own running costs and the staff wages for the building

knowledgeChecks.question: How should a US pay share or a US tax reporting rule in a source be treated in an Australian course?
options: Apply it to Australian trainers as it stands without checking it at all
Convert it to Australian dollars at the current exchange rate
Record it as US and historical, and do not use it as an Australian fact
